title: Ysolde and the Teapot of Tricks
markdown:
In the kingdom of the Glimmering Peaks, rope bridges swayed like dragon’s tails over ravines, and lanterns laid gold on winding goat paths. Some places feel awake. At the heart of it lived an ogre named Ysolde. Large, as ogres tend to be: shoulders broad as a mountain’s flank, hands that could span a dinner plate when they were not tending moonpetal herbs. Under the sturdy frame, a spirit as gentle as alpine breeze. She found more joy in a new leaf unfurling than in any clamor. Her greatest companion was Nip, a snow hare white as the highest drift, whose twitching ears seemed to catch feelings as well as sounds.

One blustery morning a flustered messenger arrived, puffing cheeks, flapping cloak, muddy prints on her meticulously swept stone steps.

“The Annual Glimmering Peaks Festival,” he gasped. “The judges have all come down with festive sniffles. The elders implore you, Ogre Ysolde, to lend your esteemed presence as judge for the Most Marvelous Manifestation contest.”

Ysolde had been humming to newly sprouted glow-roots. Judge. A festival. Noise. Hustle. Far too many people. She preferred damp earth and blooming herbs to roasted nuts and nervous sweat. She hesitated. Nip nudged her ankle, insistent. Ears twitching, a silent push.

Ysolde sighed, a puff of mist. “Very well. But Nip comes too. He has a good eye for detail.”

The messenger bowed clumsily and fled, leaving her to ponder the impending pandemonium.

The festival grounds were a riot of colour and sound, just as she had feared. Crimson and gold banners snapping. Music spilling from every tent. Faces bright with anticipation. The goat paths had been raked, then immediately unraked by boots. Dizzying, for someone used to the order of a garden. Ysolde walked the rows as if they were beds of herbs, slow on purpose, Nip’s claws a small punctuation on her shoulder. The entries were marvelous in the way mountain folk can be marvelous. A cloud woven into a tapestry that, when touched, rained tiny edible sugar plums. Chimes that played the laughter of mountain winds. A crystal that showed fleeting happy memories, including one of a child losing a tooth and looking proud about it. Ysolde took notes in a hand too large for the pencil. She even managed a private smile at a squirrel carved juggling acorns.

Then a small wiry goblin named Fizzwick Glimmerduster stepped forward, jerky as a spark. He was known throughout the peaks for his entrepreneurial spirit.

“Behold,” he crowed, raspy. “The Infinite Infuser of Instantaneous Idyllicity.”

He held up a plain grey roughly made teapot. Utterly unremarkable. The crowd murmured. Ysolde’s brow furrowed.

“But what does it do?” asked a curious dwarf.

Fizzwick winked. “It produces precisely what the heart desires at the exact moment it desires it. A solution to every fleeting lack. No more waiting. No more wishing. Just having.”

He poured water from a nearby pitcher, thought aloud of a perfect cup of spiced mountain tea, and from the spout came a steaming fragrant brew, perfectly spiced, impossibly warm. Gasps. Eager whispers. A young woman, flustered, mumbled that she wished she had not lost her favourite hairpin. Poof. A replica on a display table, tiny shimmering ruby and all.

Fizzwick’s Infinite Infuser was too perfect, and in its perfection, deeply flawed. Trinkets and comforts arrived so swiftly that people stopped caring about the other entries. A knight, eager to impress, wished for a magnificent dragon-scale shield. Clang. It appeared, glimmering, and felt strangely light, almost flimsy. Nip twitched his nose. Ysolde felt a knot in her sturdy stomach. The joy in people’s eyes was thinning, replaced by a gluttonous wish for more. Nip hopped down, nudged her hand, and pointed a tiny paw at Fizzwick, who was basking.

Ysolde looked at the hare, then at the goblin. She thought of her herb garden: careful tending, rich soil, waiting. Some plants earned their bloom. The teapot bypassed the wait. It gave you the thing and stripped the journey. The shield had not been forged. The tea had not been shared at a hearth.

“That is not a prophecy of marvel,” Ysolde said, cutting through the murmur. “That is a shopping list with ambition, nothing more.” She pointed. “Fizzwick, this teapot provides desires, not creations. A quick fix is rarely marvelous. True marvel comes from skill, from passion, from patience—qualities already on display here.”

Fizzwick spluttered, mottled green. His magic was not enchantment. Mirrors. Quick hands. The illusion of instant satisfaction, with nothing left to hold.

As the sun set, pine shadows striped the paths, amber and rose on the peaks. The festival did not end in fireworks. Someone packed the teapot away without ceremony. Villagers shared the actual sugar plums from the cloud-tapestry, juice on their fingers, no poof required. They hummed the wind-chime music. They talked about the memories in the crystal, stories that felt like they belonged to the people telling them. Ysolde, Nip curled on her lap, shared a quiet cup of spiced tea, brewed the old-fashioned way by a smiling baker who had worked his stall all day. Steam. Cinnamon. A chip in the mug. No spout that cheated. Nip’s ears went still, which was how he approved. The banners went slack in the evening wind, and the teapot, ignored at last, sat looking as ordinary as it had always been. Ysolde walked home along the goat path in the dark, herbs waiting, glow-roots unjudged, and the festival noise thinning until it was only a river far below.
audience: teenagers aged 13-15, amusing fantasy story for older readers
